body_md: A recurring complaint, always working late, never initiating plans, often sits on top of a deeper need for reassurance, closeness or respect that never gets named directly. Have each partner trace one recurring complaint back to the need underneath it, then share the need rather than the complaint. This shift in language often changes the entire tone of the conversation that follows.

fields.label: Partner A: a recurring complaint
Partner A: the need underneath it
Partner B: a recurring complaint
Partner B: the need underneath it
How naming the need changed the conversation

title: Family Feelings Weather Check Craft
summary: A child and parent each place a marker on a shared weather chart to show how the family feels that day.
goal: Give a family a simple, visual way to check in about tension at home.
body_md: Each family member places a small marker on a shared sun-to-storm chart once a day, giving the family a quick, low-pressure way to notice tension building before it becomes a bigger issue. The child gets equal say in the chart, which itself communicates that their read on the household matters. Talk briefly about any storm markers, but do not force a full conversation if no one is ready.

fields.label: Where I placed my marker today
What is behind my marker, if I want to share
Where other family members placed theirs
Something that could move the weather toward sun

title: Repair Attempt Recognition Game
summary: Partners practice spotting and rewarding each other's small repair attempts during a mock disagreement.
goal: Build a couple's ability to notice and accept a repair attempt in real time.
body_md: Have the couple act out a mild, scripted disagreement and practice inserting small repair attempts, a joke, a softer tone, reaching for a hand, then pause and name out loud when a repair attempt happened and whether it landed. Missed repair attempts are common and worth discussing without blame. Repeat with a slightly different scenario to build the recognition habit.

fields.label: A repair attempt I made
Whether my partner caught it
A repair attempt my partner made
Whether I caught it
What made a repair attempt easier or harder to notice

title: Body Safety and Choice Reclaiming Sheet
summary: Lists small, everyday choices the client can make about their own body and space to rebuild a sense of control.
goal: Rebuild a felt sense of choice and control over the client's own body, in small everyday ways.
body_md: List small, ordinary choices the client already has about their own body and personal space, what to wear, whether to hug someone hello, how close to sit to another person, and note which ones currently feel accessible versus which still feel hard to claim. This stays focused on present-day choice and control, never on recounting what happened. Build from the choices that already feel available.

fields.label: A choice about my body that feels accessible right now
A choice that still feels hard to claim
What would help make it more accessible
One small choice I will practice claiming this week
How it felt to claim it

title: Present-Day Safety Evidence Log
summary: Logs evidence from daily life that the client's current environment is safe, to counter a persistent sense of danger.
goal: Help the client's nervous system gather evidence that today is not the same as the past.
body_md: Each day, have the client note one piece of concrete evidence that their current environment and relationships are safe, a locked door, a trusted person nearby, a boundary that was respected. This builds a body of present-day evidence over time without ever asking the client to revisit or describe what happened previously. Review the accumulating log together in session.

fields.label: Today's evidence of safety
How much my body believed it, out of ten
What helped it land, if anything
What I want to notice more of this week

title: Self-Compassion for the Younger Self Practice
summary: Practices directing compassion toward a younger version of the client who went through a hard experience.
goal: Offer the client's present self a way to extend compassion to a younger self, without revisiting details.
body_md: Ask the client to picture a younger version of themselves and write what they would want that younger self to know now, without describing what happened to them. Keep the focus entirely on comfort and compassion directed at the younger self, not on narrating events. Some clients find this easier through drawing or a photo rather than direct visualization; either is fine.

fields.label: What I would want my younger self to know
How I would want to comfort them
What I notice in my body doing this practice
What my present self needs to hear too

title: Grounding Through the Body Practice
summary: A body-based grounding sequence for use when a client feels pulled out of the present moment.
goal: Give the client a reliable, body-based way back to the present when it starts to slip.
body_md: Walk through pressing feet into the floor, naming the temperature of the air, and noticing a point of contact with a chair or the ground, slowly and in session first. This is a stabilizing skill and is not paired with any request to recall or narrate past events. If the practice ever brings up thoughts of self-harm, pause and address it directly in session, with 988 (call or text) available right away.

fields.label: What I feel pressing into the floor
The temperature of the air around me
A point of contact I can notice
How grounded I feel now compared to before (0 to 10)
If thoughts of self-harm come up, what I will do (988, call or text)

title: Supporting a Partner Who Is a Survivor Sheet
summary: Helps the non-survivor partner learn what supportive, non-pressuring responses look like day to day.
goal: Give a supporting partner concrete, low-pressure ways to be helpful without pushing for more than the survivor is ready for.
body_md: The supporting partner often wants to help but is unsure what is welcome, so this has the survivor name what support currently feels good, patience with physical closeness, not asking questions, checking in without pressure, while the supporting partner names their own questions or worries separately. Keep the focus on present-day support needs, not on discussing what happened. Revisit as needs shift over time.

fields.label: Survivor: what support feels good right now
Survivor: what does not feel good right now
Supporting partner: a worry I have about getting this right
Supporting partner: what I will try instead
How this conversation felt for each of us

title: Coping Toolbox Craft
summary: A child decorates a small box and fills it with reminders of coping skills that actually work for them.
goal: Give a child a physical, personalized collection of their own working coping skills.
body_md: The parent and child decorate a small box together, then fill it with cards or small objects representing coping skills that have actually worked before, a stress ball, a breathing card, a photo of a calming place. The child picks what goes in based on their own experience, not a generic list. Keep the box somewhere easy to reach during a hard moment.

fields.label: A coping skill I put in my box
Why I picked it
Another skill I added
A time this week I used something from my box

title: Coping Skill Speed Match Game
summary: Players race to match a distressing scenario card with the coping skill card that fits it best.
goal: Build quick recall of which coping skill fits which kind of distress.
body_md: Lay out scenario cards and coping skill cards, then have players race, individually or in teams, to make the fastest correct matches, discussing any disputed pairing afterward since more than one skill can often fit. This builds quick recall under a bit of pressure, closer to how skill use actually needs to work in real moments. Close by asking each player their go-to match.

fields.label: A match I made quickly
A match that was disputed
My personal go-to skill for a tough scenario
A skill I want to get better at reaching for

title: Coping Skill Context Map
summary: Sorts a client's coping skills by the setting they are actually usable in, home, work, in public.
goal: Match coping skills to where the client can realistically use them, not just what sounds good on paper.
body_md: A coping skill that works well at home may be impossible to use discreetly at work, so this sorts the client's known skills by setting: private and unlimited, at work, in public, in front of others. Identify any setting with no usable skill yet and brainstorm one that would actually fit there. This turns a general coping list into something usable in the moment it is actually needed.

fields.label: Skills that work at home
Skills that work at work or school
Skills that work in public
A setting with no skill yet
A skill to try building for that setting

title: Coping Skill Cost and Payoff Sheet
summary: Weighs the short-term relief and longer-term cost of a client's current coping habits.
goal: Help the client see which coping habits are worth keeping and which are worth replacing.
body_md: List the client's current go-to coping habits, healthy and less healthy alike, and rate each for short-term relief and longer-term cost side by side. Some habits will score well on both, some will trade a small relief for a larger cost, and naming that plainly makes the tradeoff visible without moralizing about it. Pick one habit to work on shifting first.

fields.label: A current coping habit
Short-term relief it provides
Longer-term cost, if any
Another habit and the same rating
Which habit I want to shift first

title: Values-Matched Coping Menu
summary: Builds a coping skills menu filtered through which ones actually fit the client's values, not just what is calming.
goal: Choose coping skills that both soothe and align with the kind of life the client wants to build.
body_md: Rather than listing coping skills purely by how calming they are, have the client also rate how well each one fits the life they are trying to build, a skill that isolates the client from people who matter might soothe short term while working against a value of connection. Keep the ones that score well on both. This produces a shorter, more genuinely useful menu than a generic list.

fields.label: A coping skill and how calming it is
How well it fits my values
Another skill and the same two ratings
A skill that scores well on both
A skill I might want to swap out

title: Phobia Exposure Distress Tolerance Card
summary: A skills card to use during a planned exposure to a feared object or situation.
goal: Give the client skills to stay with a planned exposure step instead of escaping it.
body_md: List two or three skills the client will use to stay present during a planned exposure step, paced breathing, a grounding phrase, reminding themselves the goal is staying rather than feeling calm. Rehearse the card before the actual exposure happens. Log distress at the start, peak and end of the step to show the client their own pattern of the fear settling over time.

fields.label: The exposure step planned
Skill I will use to stay with it
Distress at the start
Distress at the peak
Distress at the end

title: Partner Support During Exposure Sheet
summary: Defines exactly how a partner can help during a planned exposure without accidentally rescuing.
goal: Keep a well-meaning partner's support from turning into an escape route during exposure work.
body_md: A supporting partner's instinct to comfort can accidentally let the client escape the exposure early, so this spells out exactly what helpful support looks like, staying nearby, not offering an out, a specific phrase of encouragement, versus what to avoid. Both partners agree on the plan together before the exposure happens. Debrief afterward on what actually helped.

fields.label: Client: what support helps during exposure
Client: what accidentally lets me escape
Partner: what I will say or do
Partner: what I will avoid doing
How the last exposure went with this plan

title: Brave Steps Feared Thing Chart
summary: A child builds a step-by-step chart toward a feared object or situation, adding a sticker at each step.
goal: Give a child a visible, gradual path toward a feared thing instead of an all-or-nothing leap.
body_md: The parent and child break a feared thing, a dog, the dark, a doctor visit, into small steps and build a chart together, adding a sticker each time a step is managed. The parent stays close and matches the pace to the child rather than pushing to the next step before the current one feels steady. Celebrate every step, including ones that need repeating.

fields.label: The feared thing on my chart
The step I am working on
How scared I felt (small, medium, big)
The sticker I earned
The next step on my chart

title: Fear Fact Check Game
summary: Players sort statements about a feared object into facts and fear-driven exaggerations.
goal: Separate the real facts about a feared object from what fear has exaggerated.
body_md: Prepare a set of statements about a commonly feared object or situation, some accurate and some exaggerated by fear, and have players sort them while discussing why fear tends to distort in that particular direction. This works especially well in a group where members share the same or different phobias. Close with each player's own fear-driven exaggeration and its more accurate counterpart.

fields.label: A statement I correctly sorted as fact
A statement I correctly sorted as exaggeration
My own fear-driven exaggeration about my feared thing
A more accurate version of that same statement

title: Fear Hierarchy Refresh Sheet
summary: Revisits and updates an existing exposure hierarchy as steps become easier or new ones become relevant.
goal: Keep a fear hierarchy current instead of letting it go stale as progress happens.
body_md: A hierarchy built weeks ago often no longer matches where the client actually is, so this has the client re-rate each step's current distress level and add any new steps that have become relevant since. Steps that have dropped in distress can be marked complete, and steps that never got attempted can be reconsidered. This keeps exposure work matched to real, current progress.

fields.label: A step whose distress rating has changed
New distress rating for it
A step I have not attempted yet
A new step to add to the hierarchy
The next step to work on

title: Appearance Talk Reduction Log
summary: Tracks how often a client's day involves appearance-focused talk or thought, without judgment.
goal: Build awareness of how much daily attention appearance talk is actually taking up.
body_md: Have the client note, without judging the count, every time appearance came up in their own thinking or in conversation with others across a day. Awareness alone often starts to shift the habit before any active change is asked for. Use the log to spot one specific moment or conversation pattern worth working on directly.

fields.label: A moment appearance came up in my thinking today
A moment it came up in conversation
How many times total, roughly
A pattern I noticed across the week
One moment I want to work on changing

title: Body as Instrument Practice
summary: Practices describing the body by what it does and enables rather than by how it looks.
goal: Shift attention from appearance to function as a different, workable relationship with the body.
body_md: Have the client list what their body actually lets them do across a typical day, carrying groceries, hugging someone, walking somewhere they wanted to go, without any reference to appearance. This is a genuine shift in attention, not a trick to force positivity, and some days will feel easier than others. Revisit the list regularly rather than writing it once.

fields.label: Something my body let me do today
Another thing
A way my body has supported me over the years
How it felt to describe my body this way
What I want to notice more of tomorrow

title: Mirror Time Limit Practice
summary: Practices a brief, timed mirror check paired with a grounding skill instead of an open-ended one.
goal: Interrupt a pattern of extended mirror-checking with a bounded, skills-paired alternative.
body_md: Extended mirror-checking often increases distress rather than resolving it, so this sets a short time limit for any mirror check, thirty seconds works for many clients, followed immediately by a grounding or self-soothing skill. Log how often the urge to check longer showed up and how the paired skill affected it. This is a gradual practice and does not need to be perfect from day one.

fields.label: A mirror check today and how long it lasted
The skill I paired with it
The urge to check longer, rated 0 to 10
How I felt right after using the skill
What I noticed by the end of the week

title: Partner Appearance Comment Agreement
summary: Has a couple agree on how appearance gets talked about, or not, between them.
goal: Give a couple a shared, explicit agreement about appearance comments instead of leaving it unspoken.
body_md: Well-meaning appearance comments, even compliments, can land badly for a partner working on their body image, so this has both partners name what kind of comments actually help, what kind do not, and agree on an alternative way to express care that does not center appearance at all. Revisit if either partner notices the agreement slipping. Keep the tone collaborative rather than restrictive.

fields.label: Partner A: appearance comments that help
Partner A: appearance comments that do not help
Partner B: appearance comments that help
Partner B: appearance comments that do not help
A non-appearance way we will express care instead

title: Bodies Do Many Things Drawing
summary: A child draws themselves doing several favorite activities to connect their body to what it can do.
goal: Help a child build an early, function-focused relationship with their own body.
body_md: The parent and child draw the child doing a handful of favorite activities, climbing, dancing, drawing itself, and talk about what the body was doing in each picture rather than how it looked. This plants an early function-focused frame for body image before appearance-focused messages take hold more strongly. Keep the conversation light and led by what the child brings up.

fields.label: An activity I drew myself doing
What my body was doing in that picture
Another activity I drew
How my body helped me do it
My favorite thing my body lets me do

title: Digital Habits Awareness Log
summary: Tracks when and why a client reaches for a phone to spot the habit underneath the habit.
goal: Help a client notice the triggers and payoffs behind automatic phone use.
body_md: Screens are often reached for automatically, so this has a client log a handful of pickups each day: the moment before, the feeling driving it, and what happened right after. Patterns tend to surface within a few days, such as reaching for a phone whenever a task feels hard or a room goes quiet. Use the log to open a conversation about which habits the client wants to keep and which they would rather change, kept collaborative rather than a strict rule.

fields.label: A moment today I picked up my phone without thinking
What I was feeling or avoiding right before
What I got out of it
A pickup I noticed was actually useful
One pattern I want to try changing

title: Forgiveness Process Worksheet
summary: Walks a client through what forgiveness would and would not mean for a specific hurt.
goal: Help a client sort out what letting go of a grudge would actually involve.
body_md: Forgiveness is often confused with excusing harm or reopening contact, so this worksheet separates the two: what the client would keep holding a person accountable for, and what they might set down for their own sake. There is no timeline attached and no expectation that the client reach a conclusion in one sitting. Some clients decide forgiveness is not the goal, and that is a legitimate place to land too.

fields.label: The situation I am thinking about
What I am still angry or hurt about
What forgiving would not mean for me
What forgiving might mean for me, if anything
What I need before I could consider it

title: Life Chapter Compass
summary: Maps what a client wants to carry forward and leave behind during a major life change.
goal: Give a client a structured way to think through a transition instead of just reacting to it.
body_md: A move, a job change, a divorce or a new chapter of any kind can leave a client reacting to logistics without ever stepping back to ask what they actually want from the change. This worksheet has them name what from the old chapter is worth keeping, what they are relieved to leave, and what they hope the next chapter includes. Revisit it partway through the transition, since answers often shift once the change is underway.

fields.label: The transition I am in or facing
What I want to carry forward from before
What I am relieved to be leaving behind
What I hope this next chapter includes
One small step that would move me toward it

title: Decision Fatigue Reset Sheet
summary: Helps a client trim the number of daily decisions draining their energy.
goal: Reduce the mental load of small daily decisions so a client has more energy for what matters.
body_md: By the end of a long day, small decisions like what to eat or wear can feel as hard as the big ones, which is a common sign of decision fatigue rather than a personal failing. This sheet has a client list the decisions that repeat every day and pick a handful to simplify or automate, such as a standing lunch rotation or laying out clothes the night before. The goal is fewer decisions overall, not more discipline.

fields.label: Small decisions that repeat almost every day for me
One decision I could automate or simplify
One decision I could hand off or drop entirely
How I expect to feel with fewer decisions to make
What I will try this week

title: Work-Life Boundary Map
summary: Has a client draw where work currently bleeds into personal time and where they want a firmer line.
goal: Give a client a visual starting point for setting boundaries around work hours.
body_md: Many clients describe work as having no edges, checking messages at dinner or before sleep without quite deciding to. This map has a client sketch a typical day and mark where work currently spills over, then mark where they would like a firmer edge instead. Keep the first pass realistic rather than ideal, and revisit it once a new boundary has had a week or two to be tested.

fields.label: A typical weekday, roughly hour by hour
Where work currently spills into personal time
One edge I want to hold more firmly
What might make that edge hard to hold
A support that would make it easier

title: Mind Reading Evidence Check
summary: Separates what a client actually knows about another person's thoughts from what they assumed.
goal: Help a client catch the thinking trap of assuming they know what someone else is thinking.
body_md: Assuming another person's thoughts without checking is one of the more common thinking traps, and it tends to run in one direction, usually toward a negative guess. This sheet has a client write the assumption, then list the actual evidence for it, and finally consider one or two other explanations that fit the same facts equally well. Over repeated use, clients often notice the gap between how confident the guess felt and how little evidence backed it.

fields.label: What I assumed the other person was thinking
How confident I felt about that guess, 0 to 10
The actual evidence I have for it
Another explanation that fits just as well
How I could check instead of guess

title: Fortune Telling Evidence Log
summary: Logs predicted outcomes against what actually happened to weaken the habit of forecasting doom.
goal: Show a client the gap between predicted outcomes and what actually occurs.
body_md: Predicting how a situation will go before it happens, almost always toward the worst case, keeps a client bracing for things that often do not occur. This log has them write a prediction before an event and the actual outcome afterward, side by side. Over a week or two the pattern usually becomes visible on the page itself, which tends to land better than being told the predictions are inaccurate.

fields.label: The situation I am about to face
My prediction for how it will go
How confident I am in that prediction, 0 to 10
What actually happened
What I notice comparing the two

title: Labeling Language Swap
summary: Rewrites a global self-label as a specific, changeable behavior instead.
goal: Help a client trade a fixed self-label for language that describes behavior, not identity.
body_md: A single mistake can turn into a global label like calling oneself lazy or a failure, which tends to flatten a specific event into a fixed identity. This sheet has a client write the label they reached for, then rewrite it as a specific behavior in a specific moment instead. The rewrite is not meant to excuse the behavior, only to describe it in a way that leaves room for it to be different next time.

fields.label: The label I called myself
The specific moment or behavior it was actually about
A description of that moment without the label attached
What I would want to do differently next time
One thing that label leaves out about me

title: All-or-Nothing Scale Practice
summary: Has a client place a black-and-white judgment onto a 0 to 10 scale to find the middle ground.
goal: Loosen all-or-nothing thinking by practicing a graded scale instead of two extremes.
body_md: All-or-nothing thinking sorts a day, a relationship or a performance into only two bins, total success or total failure, which leaves no room for the middle ground where most of life actually happens. This practice has a client take a recent either-or judgment and place it on a 0 to 10 scale instead, then name what specifically earned it that number rather than a 0 or a 10. Repeating this with several judgments over a week usually starts to loosen the habit.

fields.label: The all-or-nothing judgment I made
Where it lands on a 0 to 10 scale instead of two extremes
What specifically earned it that number
What would move it up one point
What I notice using a scale instead of two boxes

title: Discounting the Positive Log
summary: Tracks moments a client waved off something good so the pattern becomes visible.
goal: Help a client notice how often they dismiss positive events or feedback in the moment.
body_md: Discounting the positive shows up as a quick mental edit, a compliment gets rephrased as politeness or a good outcome gets credited to luck, and it happens fast enough that clients rarely notice it in real time. This log asks a client to catch the moment right after it happens and write both the original event and the discount that followed. Reading the list back at the end of the week is often more persuasive than pointing it out in session.

fields.label: Something good that happened or was said to me today
How I discounted or waved it off in the moment
What I would say if a friend discounted it that way
A version of the event without the discount attached
What I notice across the week's entries

title: Sailboat in the Storm Metaphor
summary: Uses a sailboat unable to control the weather to talk about steering toward values instead.
goal: Give a client a metaphor for acting on values while difficult feelings are present, not after they pass.
body_md: A sailor cannot control the wind or the waves, only the direction of the sail, and that image gives a client language for the difference between controlling a feeling and choosing a direction despite it. Talk through what the client's current storm looks like and what steering toward values would look like inside it rather than after it clears. The point is not to calm the storm before moving; it is to move while it is happening.

fields.label: What storm I am currently sailing through
What I have been trying to control that I cannot
The direction I actually want to steer toward
What steering that way would look like this week
What I can adjust, even if the storm does not calm

title: Man in the Hole Metaphor
summary: Uses digging a bigger hole with the only tool on hand to talk about when a coping strategy stops working.
goal: Help a client notice when a familiar coping strategy has become the thing digging the hole deeper.
body_md: A person stuck in a hole with only a shovel keeps digging because it is the only tool they have, even though digging makes the hole deeper, and the metaphor gives a client a nonjudgmental way to talk about a coping strategy that no longer helps. Name the strategy together, what it was meant to solve, and what putting the shovel down and trying something else might look like. This works best held lightly rather than as a verdict on the client.

fields.label: The hole I feel stuck in
The shovel, or strategy, I keep reaching for
What that strategy was originally trying to solve
What putting the shovel down might look like
A different tool I could try instead

title: Career Transition Values Sheet
summary: Grounds a career change in values instead of only in salary or title.
goal: Help a client weigh a career decision against what actually matters to them.
body_md: A career change is often framed purely in terms of salary, title or prestige, which can leave a client feeling unsettled even after landing an objectively good offer. This sheet has a client name the values they want their work to serve, then hold each option they are weighing up against those values rather than against each other directly. It is meant to sit alongside practical factors, not replace them.

fields.label: The career decision or transition in front of me
The values I want my work to serve
How each option lines up with those values
What a purely practical decision might miss
What I am leaning toward and why

title: Retirement Identity Values Practice
summary: Helps a client separate their sense of self from a job title they are about to lose.
goal: Support a client in finding identity and values beyond a role that is ending.
body_md: Retirement can remove a role a client has organized much of their identity around for decades, and the loss of structure and purpose often surprises people who expected only to feel relief. This practice has a client name what the role gave them beyond a paycheck, such as purpose, contact with people or a sense of competence, and then explore other ways those same needs could be met going forward. Go slowly; this can bring up grief alongside relief.

fields.label: What my work role gave me beyond income
What I am relieved to be leaving behind
What I am grieving or unsure about losing
Another way I could meet that same need going forward
What I want this next chapter to be about

title: Forgiveness as Willingness Practice
summary: Reframes forgiveness as a willingness to stop carrying a struggle rather than a verdict about another person.
goal: Help a client consider forgiveness as an act of willingness rather than a judgment they owe someone else.
body_md: Forgiveness debates often get stuck on whether the other person deserves it, which can keep a client carrying a struggle indefinitely while waiting for an answer that may never come. This practice reframes forgiveness as a willingness question aimed at the client's own life: am I willing to stop carrying this, for my own sake, regardless of what the other person deserves. There is no requirement to reach a yes, only to look at the question honestly.

fields.label: What I am carrying that relates to this person
What carrying it is costing me
Whether willingness to set it down feels possible right now
What setting it down would and would not mean
One value it would free me up to move toward

title: Choosing Acceptance Again Practice
summary: Practices the repeated choice to turn toward acceptance of a fact a client cannot change.
goal: Give a client a concrete way to practice choosing acceptance again and again, not just once.
body_md: Turning the mind is less a single decision than a repeated one, like standing at a fork in the road and choosing the accepting path over and over as the mind wanders back toward fighting a fact. This card has a client name a fact they are working on accepting and practice noticing the moment they turn away from it, then gently turn back. It rarely happens once and is complete; expect it to be a return, not a finish line.

fields.label: The fact I am practicing accepting
A moment today I turned away from accepting it
What turning back toward acceptance looked like
How many times I noticed the choice today
What made turning back easier or harder

title: Building a Life Worth Living Plan
summary: Has a client sketch what more of their life would need to include to feel worth living day to day.
goal: Give a client a concrete, ongoing picture of the life they are working toward, not just the crisis they are managing.
body_md: Skills work can end up entirely focused on managing crises, which leaves little room to talk about what the client actually wants their life to include. This plan has a client name what currently makes life worth living, what is missing, and one step toward adding more of it in. If low points or thoughts of self-harm come up while building this plan, complete this in session, and name that 988 can be called or texted anytime the client needs support between sessions.

fields.label: What currently makes my life feel worth living
What is missing that I wish were there
One value or activity I want more of in my life
A small step toward adding it in this month
Who or what I can lean on along the way

title: Willingness vs Willfulness Check
summary: Helps a client tell the difference between digging in against reality and cooperating with it.
goal: Help a client notice when they are fighting a situation rather than working with it.
body_md: Willfulness looks like refusing to do what is needed, crossing arms and insisting reality should be different, while willingness looks like doing what the moment calls for even when it is unwelcome. This check has a client notice a current stuck point and ask which stance they are in, then consider what one willing action might look like even without feeling ready. Naming the stance out loud often loosens it on its own.

fields.label: The situation I feel stuck in
Signs I am in a willful stance right now
What willingness would look like here instead
One small willing action I could take
What is making willingness hard right now

title: IMPROVE the Moment Card
summary: A pocket card of ways to make a hard moment more bearable without needing it to be over.
goal: Give a client a quick menu of ways to get through a hard moment rather than escape it.
body_md: Some moments cannot be shortened or avoided, only gotten through, and this card offers a short menu of ways to make that getting-through a little more bearable: imagery, meaning, a brief prayer or reflection, relaxing the body, one thing at a time, a short vacation from the problem, and encouragement to oneself. A client picks whichever one or two fit the moment rather than working through the whole list in order.

fields.label: The hard moment I am in
Which idea on the card I am drawn to right now
What using it looked like
How the moment felt afterward, 0 to 10
Which idea I want to remember for next time

title: Observe Describe Participate Practice
summary: Practices the three mindfulness what-skills in a short daily sequence.
goal: Build fluency with the observe, describe and participate skills as a short daily sequence.
body_md: Observing, describing and participating are the three what-skills of mindfulness, and practicing them in a fixed short sequence, first just noticing, then putting words to it, then stepping fully into the activity, helps them become more automatic over time. This card walks a client through the sequence with any ordinary moment, a meal, a walk, a conversation. Keep it brief; a minute of each step is enough to build the habit.

fields.label: What I am observing right now, without judging it
How I would describe it in plain words
What fully participating in this moment looks like
What pulled my attention away, if anything
How this felt compared with going on autopilot

title: Blended Family Roles Sheet
summary: Has both partners name what role each wants with the other's children before conflicts force the question.
goal: Give a blended family couple a shared, explicit picture of each partner's role instead of an assumed one.
body_md: Blended families often run into conflict when partners have never actually discussed what role a stepparent should play with the other's children, discipline especially, and each partner has been operating on an unstated assumption. This sheet has both partners describe what role they want and what role they think would help the children, then compare notes and agree on a starting point. Expect to revisit it as the family settles in.

fields.label: Partner A: the role I want to play with the children
Partner A: where I want to defer to my partner
Partner B: the role I want to play with the children
Partner B: where I want to defer to my partner
One agreement we are making for now

title: Long-Distance Connection Plan
summary: Has a couple build a concrete plan for staying connected across distance and time zones.
goal: Give a long-distance couple a shared, concrete plan instead of leaving connection to chance.
body_md: Distance strips out the small, ordinary contact that keeps most couples connected, so this plan has both partners name what kind of contact they actually want, calls, messages, shared shows or games, and agree on a rough rhythm that fits both schedules and time zones. Revisit the plan when either partner's routine changes. The goal is a plan both partners chose, not one imposed by whoever misses the other more.

fields.label: Partner A: the kind of contact I want most
Partner A: what has been hardest about the distance
Partner B: the kind of contact I want most
Partner B: what has been hardest about the distance
A rhythm of contact we are agreeing to try

title: Money Values Comparison Sheet
summary: Has both partners name what money means to them before working out shared spending decisions.
goal: Help a couple talk about the values behind money before the numbers themselves.
body_md: Money arguments are often really values arguments, one partner spending toward security and the other toward experience, without either naming it that way. This sheet has each partner describe what money represents to them, safety, freedom, generosity, before moving to any specific budget conversation. Understanding the value underneath a spending habit usually makes the practical negotiation that follows much easier.

fields.label: Partner A: what money represents to me
Partner A: a spending habit that reflects that value
Partner B: what money represents to me
Partner B: a spending habit that reflects that value
Where our values overlap or differ

title: Career Transition Team Planning Sheet
summary: Has a couple plan together how a job change, move or return to school will be shared between them.
goal: Give a couple a shared plan for absorbing the load of one partner's career transition.
body_md: A career change, whether a new job, a return to school or a move, usually reshapes both partners' daily lives, not just the one making the change, and unspoken expectations about who picks up the slack can cause resentment. This sheet has both partners name what will shift, who will carry which tasks during the transition, and when to check back in. Treat the plan as a draft to be adjusted once the transition is underway.

fields.label: Partner A: how this transition affects my daily life
Partner A: what I am willing to take on during it
Partner B: how this transition affects my daily life
Partner B: what I am willing to take on during it
When we will check back in on how it is going

title: Friendship Circle Balance Check
summary: Has both partners map their outside friendships to see if either feels isolated from support outside the relationship.
goal: Help a couple notice whether one or both partners have let outside friendships lapse.
body_md: A relationship that becomes each partner's only source of support can end up carrying more weight than it can hold, so this check has both partners map who else they lean on and how often. Compare notes on whether either partner's circle has thinned out since the relationship began, and talk about what would help rebuild it without either partner feeling threatened by the other's outside friendships.

fields.label: Partner A: who I lean on outside this relationship
Partner A: how that circle has changed over time
Partner B: who I lean on outside this relationship
Partner B: how that circle has changed over time
One step either of us could take to reconnect with a friend

title: New Sibling Adjustment Book
summary: A child makes a small book about becoming a big sibling to process the change.
goal: Help a young child put words and pictures to the changes a new sibling brings.
body_md: A new baby reshapes a young child's world, attention especially, and this has the parent and child make a simple book together with a page for feelings about the baby, a page for what stays the same, and a page for a special job only the older sibling gets to do. Let the child dictate or draw rather than correcting their answers. Revisit the book in the weeks after the baby arrives.

fields.label: A page about how I feel about the new baby
A page about something that stays the same for me
A page about my special big-sibling job
A page about something I am excited about
A page about something that feels hard right now

title: First Day Jitters Plan
summary: A child and parent build a simple plan for a nervous first day at a new school or activity.
goal: Give a nervous child a concrete plan to hold onto before a first day.
body_md: A first day at a new school, camp or activity can bring up big nerves that are hard for a young child to put into words, and having a concrete plan in hand tends to help more than reassurance alone. The parent and child draw out what the morning will look like step by step, and agree on one small comfort item or phrase the child can use if they feel scared. Practice the plan out loud together before the day arrives.

fields.label: What I am nervous about
What the morning will look like, step by step
My comfort item or phrase for if I feel scared
Who I can look for if I need help
One thing I am a little excited about

title: Screen Time Family Agreement Craft
summary: A child decorates a household screen time agreement they helped write.
goal: Give a family a screen time agreement the child had a hand in creating.
body_md: A screen time rule the child helped write tends to stick better than one simply handed down, so the parent and child talk through when screens are and are not used, then the child decorates a poster listing the agreement to hang somewhere visible. Keep the child's input genuine on at least a few points, even if the parent sets the outer limits. Revisit the poster if it stops matching what actually happens.

fields.label: Times screens are okay in our house
Times screens are not okay in our house
What I want to do instead during no-screen times
What happens if the agreement is not followed
How I decorated my poster

title: Growth Mindset Poster Craft
summary: A child illustrates the difference between not being able to do something yet and never.
goal: Help a child build language for approaching a hard task as a skill still in progress.
body_md: Young children often treat a hard task as proof they simply cannot do it, and this craft gives them a concrete way to add the word yet to that sentence instead. The child draws or writes something they find hard now next to a picture of what it might look like once they have practiced it more. Keep the poster somewhere visible and refer back to it the next time a task feels too hard.

fields.label: Something that feels hard for me right now
What I say to myself when it feels hard
What I could say instead, adding the word yet
A time I got better at something with practice
What I drew for my poster

title: Kindness Tally Chain Craft
summary: A child builds a paper chain of kind acts done or received to make kindness visible over time.
goal: Give a child a visible, growing record of kindness given and received.
body_md: Kindness can feel abstract to a young child, so this craft has them add a paper link to a growing chain each time they do or notice a kind act, writing or drawing what happened on the link. The chain grows across a week or two and becomes something the child can see and be proud of. Keep the focus on noticing kindness rather than turning it into a reward system.

fields.label: A kind thing I did today
A kind thing someone did for me today
How it felt to add a new link to the chain
Who I want to be kind to tomorrow
How long my chain has grown

title: Gratitude Circle Toss
summary: A group tosses a soft ball, naming something they are grateful for each time they catch it.
goal: Give a group a quick, moving way to practice noticing and naming gratitude out loud.
body_md: Sitting still and writing a gratitude list can feel like a chore to a group, so this game keeps it moving: players toss a soft ball around a circle, and whoever catches it names one thing they are grateful for before tossing it on. Keep the pace quick and playful, and allow repeats since younger groups often circle back to favorites. Debrief briefly on whether anything surprised the group.

fields.label: Something I named when I caught the ball
Something someone else said that stuck with me
Whether gratitude got easier or harder to name as we went
One thing I noticed about the group's answers
Something I am grateful for that I did not get to say

title: Change and Transition Card Sort Game
summary: A group sorts cards describing common reactions to change into which ones feel familiar.
goal: Normalize a range of reactions to change by sorting them as a group activity.
body_md: Change brings up a wide range of reactions, relief, grief, excitement and dread often all at once, and this game has a group sort cards printed with different reactions into piles of familiar, unfamiliar and surprising. Debrief on how differently people react to the same kind of change and why that variety makes sense rather than being a sign anyone is reacting wrongly. Keep the tone curious rather than clinical.

fields.label: A reaction card that felt very familiar to me
A reaction card that surprised me
A change I am currently going through
Which cards from the sort apply to that change for me
What I noticed about how differently the group reacted

title: Team Trust Walk Game
summary: Pairs take turns guiding a blindfolded partner through a simple obstacle course, then debrief on trust.
goal: Give a group a hands-on experience of giving and receiving trust to debrief afterward.
body_md: One partner is blindfolded and guided by the other through a simple, safe obstacle course using only voice instructions, then the pair switches roles. Keep the course genuinely safe and check in before starting that both partners consent to the exercise. The debrief afterward, on what made trusting easy or hard and what made guiding easy or hard, usually carries more weight than the walk itself.

fields.label: What it felt like to be guided
What it felt like to guide someone else
What made trusting my partner easier or harder
What made giving clear guidance easier or harder
How this connects to trust outside the game

title: Feelings Detective Board Game
summary: Players move around a simple board naming feeling clues to earn a magnifying glass token.
goal: Build a young child's feeling-word vocabulary through a playful board game format.
body_md: Players take turns rolling a die and moving around a simple board, and each landing space shows a feeling clue, a facial expression or a short scenario, that the player names to earn a magnifying glass token. Keep the pace light and celebratory rather than quiz-like, and offer hints freely for younger players. Whoever collects the most tokens by the end wins, though the naming practice is the real point.

fields.label: A feeling clue I figured out during the game
A feeling that was hard for me to name
A time I actually felt one of the feelings from the board
How many tokens I collected
A new feeling word I learned

title: Values Bingo
summary: A group plays bingo with values instead of numbers to spark conversation about what matters to each player.
goal: Use a familiar bingo format to get a group talking about personal values.
body_md: Each player gets a bingo card filled with values instead of numbers, connection, honesty, adventure, and marks a square whenever that value comes up as meaningful to them during a round of quick sharing. The game rewards genuine reflection over speed, so keep rounds unhurried. Debrief on which values came up most for the group and which felt more personal or surprising.

fields.label: A value I marked on my card and why
A value on my card I was surprised to connect with
A value that did not resonate with me at all
Whether I got bingo, and on which values
One value I want to act on more this week

title: Body-Based Safety Cues Checklist
summary: Lists physical and environmental cues a client can use to confirm the present moment is safe.
goal: Give a client a quick physical checklist for confirming safety in the here and now.
body_md: When a trigger pulls attention into the past, a fast physical checklist can help a client confirm what is actually true right now: doors locked, feet on the floor, a name and today's date recalled out loud. This is meant to be completed in session first so the clinician can see what lands, then carried as a card the client can use on their own. It is a grounding tool, not a place to recount what happened.

fields.label: Cues I checked to confirm I am safe right now
What helped me feel most anchored in the present
What I will say to myself when I use this card
Where I will keep this checklist
Who I can call if grounding alone is not enough

title: Present-Tense Anchoring Sheet
summary: Practices naming five present-moment facts to interrupt a shift into past-tense activation.
goal: Help a client build a quick, repeatable way to return attention to the present moment.
body_md: A trigger can pull attention into a past moment so quickly that a client only notices after they are already activated, so this sheet practices a fast return: naming today's date, the room, and five things currently visible, out loud or on paper. Practice it in session while calm first so it is familiar before it is needed. This is a grounding skill, not a place to describe what happened.

fields.label: Today's date and where I am right now
Five things I can see right now
One thing that tells me this moment is different from then
How activated I felt before and after, 0 to 10
When I will practice this on my own this week

title: Anchored in the Room Practice
summary: Uses defusion language to separate a trauma memory from the present physical room.
goal: Help a client notice a memory as a mental event happening now, separate from the room they are actually in.
body_md: A flashback can feel like the past is happening again, and this practice uses simple defusion language, noticing 'I am having the memory that,' paired with naming the actual room, to help a client hold both facts at once: the memory is present, and so is the room. This is a stabilizing practice for the present moment, not an invitation to describe the memory's content.

fields.label: The phrase I used to notice the memory as a memory
Three facts about the actual room I am in
How holding both at once felt
What helped the most
When I could use this phrase again this week

title: Trauma Activation TIPP Card
summary: A pocket card of fast body-based skills for calming intense activation in the moment.
goal: Give a client a fast physical way to bring down intense activation before it escalates further.
body_md: When activation spikes fast, changing body temperature, intense exercise, paced breathing or paired muscle relaxation can bring the nervous system down more quickly than talking it through. This card lists each option briefly so a client can reach for whichever is available, a cold splash of water, a short fast walk, slow counted breaths. Practice each option once in session so none of them are unfamiliar when they are actually needed.

fields.label: Which skill on the card I used
My activation level before, 0 to 10
My activation level after, 0 to 10
Where I was and what was available to me
Which skill I want to keep close by

title: Partner Debrief After Activation Sheet
summary: Gives both partners a short, structured way to check in after one partner has a triggered moment.
goal: Help a couple debrief after an activation episode without either partner having to relive the details.
body_md: After a triggered moment passes, partners often do not know what to say, either overexplaining or avoiding it entirely, and this sheet offers a short structure instead: what helped, what did not, and what the surviving partner needs going forward. It intentionally does not ask what triggered the moment or what the memory contained. Keep it brief and check in again once both partners feel settled.

fields.label: Partner A: what helped me during that moment
Partner A: what I need from my partner afterward
Partner B: what I noticed and did during that moment
Partner B: what I want to understand better for next time
One thing we will try differently next time

title: Worry Postponement Trial Card
summary: Has a client set a daily worry appointment and defer intrusive worry to it during the day.
goal: Teach a client to defer worry to a set time rather than suppress or follow it immediately.
body_md: Trying to stop a worry outright often backfires, so this card has a client note the worry briefly when it shows up and defer full attention to a fixed fifteen-minute worry appointment later that day. Many worries lose urgency by the time the appointment arrives. Track what happens at the appointment itself, since that is where the real practice happens.

fields.label: A worry I noted and deferred today
What time my worry appointment was
Whether the worry still felt urgent at that time
What I did with it during the appointment
What I noticed across the week

title: Anxious Mind Radio Station Practice
summary: Uses a radio station metaphor to help a client notice anxious thoughts without tuning in fully.
goal: Give a client a defusion tool for noticing anxious thoughts as background noise rather than instructions.
body_md: Anxious thoughts can play on a loop like a radio station a client did not choose to tune into, and this practice has them notice the broadcast without turning up the volume: 'Radio Anxiety is playing that thought again.' Naming it this way creates a small gap between the client and the thought, enough room to keep acting on what matters even while the station keeps playing.

fields.label: The anxious thought playing on the station today
What I noticed when I named it as a broadcast
What I did instead of turning up the volume
How much room that gap created, 0 to 10
What I want to keep doing even while the station plays

title: Worry Cloud Watching Craft
summary: A child draws their worry as changing weather to show that feelings pass and shift.
goal: Give a child a concrete image for understanding that anxious feelings change and pass.
body_md: Young children often experience worry as permanent, so this craft has them draw their worry as a weather report, stormy, cloudy, sunny, and make a few panels showing how it has changed across a day or week. Talk with the parent about noticing and naming the weather together at home. The goal is showing the child that feelings move, not fixing the weather itself.

fields.label: My worry weather today
What made the weather change during the day
A time my worry weather turned sunnier
Who I can tell when my weather feels stormy
What I drew for today's forecast

title: Worry or Fact Sorting Relay
summary: Teams race to sort statement cards into worries and facts before a group debrief.
goal: Use a fast-paced sorting relay to practice telling a worry apart from a verified fact.
body_md: Two teams race to sort a stack of cards, some worries and some verified facts, into the correct pile before time runs out, then the group reviews the sort together and discusses any cards that were tricky. Keep the pace lively and the cards realistic to the group's own worries where possible. The debrief matters more than who wins the relay.

fields.label: A card I sorted quickly
A card that was tricky to sort
What made the difference between a worry and a fact
A worry of my own I could sort this way
What I noticed about how the group did

title: Anxiety Vulnerability Factors Check
summary: Tracks sleep, food, substance use and physical strain to spot what raises anxiety's baseline.
goal: Help a client notice the physical factors that make anxiety easier or harder to manage on a given day.
body_md: Anxiety is easier to ride out on some days than others, often because of factors that have nothing to do with the worry itself: poor sleep, skipped meals, illness or physical strain. This check has a client rate a few of these factors each day alongside their anxiety level, so patterns become visible over time. It is meant to inform planning, not to explain away the anxiety entirely.

fields.label: My sleep last night, rated 0 to 10
Whether I ate regularly today
Any physical strain or illness today
My anxiety level today, 0 to 10
What I notice connecting the two

title: Getting-Up Micro-Steps Plan
summary: Breaks the first hour of the day into the smallest possible steps for a client stuck in low mood.
goal: Give a client a low-bar plan for starting the day when everything feels heavy.
body_md: When mood is very low, even a normal morning routine can feel impossible, so this plan breaks the first hour into steps small enough to actually complete: feet on the floor, one glass of water, opening the curtains. Momentum matters more than speed here. Track only whether each micro-step happened, not how the client felt about doing it.

fields.label: My micro-step plan for the first hour
Which steps I completed today
What got in the way of any I skipped
How I felt once I had done even one step
What I want to add or drop from the plan

title: Low Mood Values Anchor Card
summary: A pocket card naming one value a client can act on in a small way even on a low day.
goal: Give a client a small, values-based action to reach for on days when motivation is absent.
body_md: Waiting for motivation before acting on what matters often means waiting indefinitely when mood is low, so this card has a client identify one value, connection, care, creativity, and one tiny action that expresses it regardless of mood. The action should be small enough to be doable even on a hard day. Keep it visible somewhere the client will actually see it.

fields.label: A value I want to act on even on a low day
One tiny action that expresses it
A day I used the card
What happened when I acted despite low mood
What I want to keep on the card going forward

title: Energy Budget for Low Mood Days Sheet
summary: Helps a client allocate limited energy across a day's demands rather than pushing through all of them.
goal: Help a client triage a low-energy day instead of trying to meet every demand at full capacity.
body_md: On a low-mood day, trying to meet every ordinary demand at full capacity usually backfires and deepens the exhaustion, so this sheet has a client list the day's demands and sort them into must-do, could-shrink and can-skip. Revisiting the sheet at the end of the day, comparing plan to what actually happened, without judgment, tends to be the most useful part.

fields.label: Today's demands, listed out
Which ones truly must happen today
Which ones I could shrink to a smaller version
Which ones I can skip entirely today
How the day actually went compared with the plan

title: Partner Check-In Without Fixing Script
summary: Gives the supporting partner a script for checking in on low mood without jumping to solutions.
goal: Help a supporting partner offer presence during a low-mood stretch instead of unsolicited fixes.
body_md: A partner watching someone move through a low-mood stretch often reaches for solutions out of care, which can land as pressure rather than support. This script gives the supporting partner a few open questions to ask instead, what would help right now, do you want company or space, and a reminder to wait for an answer before offering a fix. Both partners can revise the script together.

fields.label: Supporting partner: a question I will ask instead of offering a fix
Partner with low mood: what actually helps me most right now
Partner with low mood: what does not help, even if well meant
Supporting partner: what I need in order to keep showing up
One agreement we are making about check-ins

title: Small Joys Sticker Map
summary: A child adds a sticker to a map each time they notice a small good moment during a low stretch.
goal: Help a child notice small good moments during a stretch of low mood or sadness.
body_md: A child moving through a stretch of sadness or low energy can lose track of small good moments entirely, so this map has them add a sticker to a simple drawn map each time they notice one, a favorite snack, a funny moment, a hug. The parent helps by pointing out moments the child might miss on their own. Look at the growing map together at the end of the week.

fields.label: A small good moment I noticed today
Where I put my sticker on the map
A moment my parent helped me notice
How many stickers I have so far
What I want to notice more of this week

title: Transition Warning Countdown Log
summary: Tracks how advance warnings before switching tasks affect how smoothly the switch goes.
goal: Help a client test whether advance warnings make task transitions easier to manage.
body_md: Switching between tasks can be one of the hardest parts of a day, and this log has a client try giving themselves a short warning, five or ten minutes, before a planned switch, then rate how the transition went compared with switches made with no warning. Over a week the pattern usually shows whether the warning genuinely helps or whether other supports are needed instead.

fields.label: The transition I was making
Whether I gave myself a warning beforehand
How smooth the transition felt, 0 to 10
What made it easier or harder
What I want to try differently next time

title: Values-Driven Routine Anchor
summary: Links one daily routine step to a value so it is easier to return to after it gets skipped.
goal: Help a client reconnect a dropped routine to the value it was meant to serve.
body_md: Routines built on willpower alone tend to fall apart quickly, so this practice has a client pick one routine step that keeps slipping and name the value underneath it, health, care for others, creativity, rather than the habit itself. Returning to a value after a skipped day tends to feel more workable than returning to a rule that was already broken. Track attempts rather than streaks.

fields.label: The routine step that keeps slipping
The value underneath it
A day I skipped it and what happened
A day I returned to it, even imperfectly
What returning to the value felt like versus returning to the rule

title: Emotional Flooding From Overwhelm Card
summary: A short card for when task overwhelm tips into emotional flooding rather than just distraction.
goal: Give a client a quick skill for the emotional spike that can follow ADHD-related overwhelm.
body_md: Task overwhelm can tip quickly into a genuine emotional flood, frustration, shame or panic, that then makes the original task even harder to return to. This card offers a short sequence: name the flood, use one distress tolerance skill to bring intensity down, then decide whether to return to the task or take a real break. The point is separating the emotional spike from the task itself so each can be handled on its own.

fields.label: What tipped me into flooding
The skill I used to bring intensity down
My intensity before and after, 0 to 10
Whether I returned to the task or took a break
What I want to remember for next time

title: Homework Launch Pad Craft
summary: A child decorates a homework starting kit to shrink the gap between deciding to start and actually starting.
goal: Give a child a physical kit that reduces the friction of starting homework.
body_md: The hardest part of homework for many children with attention challenges is not the work itself but the gap between deciding to start and actually starting, so this craft has the child decorate a small kit, a box or folder, holding everything needed: pencils, a timer, a fidget item. The parent helps set a consistent spot for the kit. Review together whether having it ready actually shortened the delay.

fields.label: What I put in my launch pad kit
Where I decided to keep it
How long it took me to start homework with the kit ready
What still made starting hard
One thing I want to add to the kit

title: Focus Relay Race Game
summary: Teams complete short focused tasks in relay format with brief, planned breaks built in.
goal: Practice short bursts of focus with built-in breaks through a playful relay format.
body_md: Teams take turns completing a short focused task, a puzzle piece, a simple sequence, then tag a teammate and take a planned short break before their next turn. The structure mirrors a real strategy, working in short bursts with built-in recovery, in a format that feels like play rather than a lesson. Debrief on which parts of the relay felt easiest and hardest to stay focused through.

fields.label: The task I completed during my turn
How focused I felt during my burst
What the break in between felt like
Which part of the relay was hardest to focus through
How this connects to focusing on schoolwork or chores

title: Substance Use Trigger Chain Sheet
summary: Maps the chain of events from trigger to substance use to spot an earlier point to intervene.
goal: Help a client see the chain of events leading up to substance use, not just the moment itself.
body_md: Substance use rarely happens in a single moment; it usually follows a chain, a trigger, a thought, a feeling, a decision point, that can be mapped after the fact to find an earlier place to intervene next time. This sheet has a client walk backward from a recent instance of use, naming each link, and circle the earliest point where a different choice felt possible. The goal is a map for next time, not a confession.

fields.label: The trigger that started the chain
The thought that followed
The feeling that followed
The earliest link where a different choice felt possible
What that different choice could look like next time

title: Values Beyond the Urge Practice
summary: Has a client name a value the urge is temporarily crowding out to widen the choice in the moment.
goal: Help a client notice what an urge is crowding out and reconnect with it in the moment.
body_md: An urge can narrow a client's attention until nothing else seems to matter, so this practice has them name, right in that narrowed moment, one value the urge is currently crowding out, being present for a child, staying employed, self-respect. Naming it does not make the urge disappear, but it widens the field of choice for a moment. Pair this with a concrete coping skill rather than using it alone.

fields.label: The urge I am noticing right now, 0 to 10
The value it is currently crowding out
What acting on that value would look like right now instead
What I actually did
How the urge changed afterward, if at all

title: Urge Riding Practice Card
summary: Practices noticing an urge rise, peak and fall without acting on it, timed on a simple card.
goal: Help a client build direct experience that an urge passes on its own within minutes.
body_md: An urge often feels like it will only grow unless acted on, but urges typically rise, peak and fall within a fairly short window when nothing is done to feed them. This card has a client time an urge from the moment it is noticed, rating its intensity every few minutes, to build direct evidence that it does pass. If thoughts of self-harm accompany the urge, complete this in session, and 988 can be called or texted anytime between sessions.

fields.label: The urge I am timing
Intensity at the start, 0 to 10
Intensity a few minutes in
Intensity once it had passed or eased
What I noticed about riding it out instead of acting

title: Using Alone Risk Reduction Sheet
summary: Helps a client build a safety plan for reducing risk on occasions when substance use happens alone.
goal: Give a client a concrete plan for reducing physical risk during a lapse rather than only aiming for none.
body_md: Aiming for zero use can leave no plan at all for the times use actually happens, and unplanned solo use carries more physical risk than use with another person present or aware. This sheet has a client build a concrete plan: someone to check in with, never using entirely alone, keeping naloxone accessible if relevant, and a reminder that 988 can be called or texted in a crisis. This is a safety plan, not a green light.

fields.label: Someone I can tell before I use, or check in with after
What I will keep on hand in case of an emergency
A place I will avoid using alone
My plan if things start to feel unsafe
Who else knows this plan

title: Recovery Trivia Relay Game
summary: Teams answer prompt cards about coping, triggers and support to spark group discussion.
goal: Use a light trivia format to open group discussion on coping strategies and support.
body_md: Teams take turns drawing a prompt card, naming a coping skill, a common trigger, a support person to call, and earn a point for a genuine answer rather than a technically correct one. The format keeps a heavy topic approachable and gets quieter group members talking. Spend more time on the discussion each card sparks than on keeping score.

fields.label: A prompt card I answered
A coping skill another player named that I want to try
A trigger someone mentioned that I also recognize
A support person I could add to my own list

body_md: In the moment, an angry outburst can feel like it accomplishes something, being heard, feeling powerful, ending an argument, but the actual costs often outweigh that payoff once the dust settles. This ledger has a client list both sides after a recent outburst: what it seemed to get them and what it actually cost in relationships, energy or trust. Comparing the columns side by side is usually more persuasive than being told to calm down.

body_md: Partners often make small repair attempts mid-argument, a joke, a softer tone, reaching for a hand, that go unnoticed or get rejected when tempers are already high. This sheet has each partner describe what their own repair attempts typically look like and what helps them notice and accept their partner's. Practicing recognition when calm makes it more likely to be caught in the heat of an actual argument.

body_md: In the middle of a panic surge, sensations can feel like they will last indefinitely, so this sheet has a client note their prediction for how long a sensation will last at the start, then log the actual duration once it passes. body_md: Fighting a panic sensation, trying to force it away, often intensifies it, so this practice has a client instead imagine making literal room in their body for the sensation, softening around it rather than bracing against it. This is not the same as liking the sensation or wanting it to stay; it is choosing not to add a second layer of struggle on top of the first.

body_md: A well-meaning partner can say the wrong thing during a panic episode without knowing it, telling someone to calm down rarely helps, so this sheet has both partners agree in advance on specific phrases and actions that actually help, and a short list of ones to avoid.
