title: Unspoken Rules of the Relationship Sheet
summary: Surfaces the unstated rules each partner has been operating on to check whether both actually agree to them.
goal: Help a couple name the unspoken rules quietly running their relationship and decide together whether to keep them.
body_md: Every relationship accumulates unspoken rules over time, who initiates plans, who apologizes first, what topics are off-limits, and partners often follow them without ever agreeing to them out loud. This sheet has each partner name a few rules they have noticed themselves following, then discuss together which ones both actually want to keep. Some surprise both partners once said out loud.

fields.label: Partner A: an unspoken rule I have noticed myself following
Partner A: whether I actually want to keep it
Partner B: an unspoken rule I have noticed myself following
Partner B: whether I actually want to keep it
One rule we are agreeing to change or drop

title: Relationship Thought Trap Spotter
summary: Has a client catch a thinking trap specifically about their relationship, like mind reading a partner's intent.
goal: Help a client notice thinking traps that specifically distort how they read their partner's behavior.
body_md: Thinking traps show up in relationships just as they do elsewhere, assuming a partner's silence means anger, or that one late reply means the relationship is failing, and these traps can drive a reaction before the client ever checks the facts. This sheet has a client catch a relationship-specific trap, name it, and consider a more balanced reading of the same behavior. Bring a few examples back to session.

fields.label: What my partner did or said
What I assumed it meant
The thinking trap I notice in that assumption
A more balanced reading of the same behavior
How I could check instead of assume

title: Relationship Willingness Practice
summary: Helps a client identify one values-based action toward a partner they can take despite current hurt or resentment.
goal: Help a client act on relationship values even while hurt or resentment is still present.
body_md: Waiting for hurt or resentment to fully clear before acting warmly toward a partner can mean waiting a long time, so this practice has a client identify one small values-based action, patience, warmth, honesty, they are willing to take even while the difficult feeling is still present. This is not about suppressing the feeling, only about not letting it be the only thing that decides the next action.

fields.label: The hurt or resentment currently present for me
A value I want to act on with my partner anyway
One small action that would express it
What I did
What it was like to act despite the feeling still being there

title: Relationship Distress Tolerance Menu
summary: A menu of skills a client can use to tolerate a hard relationship moment without acting impulsively.
goal: Give a client a menu of skills to reach for during a hard relationship moment instead of an impulsive reaction.
body_md: A hard moment in a relationship, a hurtful comment, a broken plan, can trigger an impulsive reaction that makes things worse before the client has had a chance to think, so this menu offers a few distress tolerance options to reach for first: a short walk, paced breathing, or naming the urge out loud before acting on it. The goal is buying time, not suppressing the feeling.

fields.label: The hard moment I am working through
The skill I reached for first
What the urge to react impulsively was telling me to do
What I did instead
How the moment looked once I had bought some time

title: Safe Adults and Safe Spaces Map
summary: Has a client map current safe people and places to build a felt sense of safety in the present.
goal: Help a client build a concrete, present-day map of safety rather than dwelling in the past.
body_md: A client working through the aftermath of sexual abuse benefits from a strong, concrete sense of who and where feels safe right now, separate from anything about what happened. This sheet has them map current safe people, places and objects, building a resource they can return to whenever grounding is needed. It is intentionally forward-facing and does not ask for any account of the past.

fields.label: A person who feels safe to me right now
A place that feels safe to me right now
An object or routine that helps me feel grounded
How I can reach one of these when I need to
What safety feels like in my body right now

title: Present-Day Body Ownership Sheet
summary: Has a client name current choices they hold over their own body to build a present-tense sense of ownership.
goal: Help a client build present-day evidence of choice and ownership over their own body.
body_md: Reclaiming a felt sense of ownership over one's own body can be a slow, present-focused process, and this sheet supports it by having a client name small choices they currently hold, what to wear, who to be touched by, how to move through their day, and notice each one as an exercise of that ownership. This stays entirely in the present and does not ask about the past.

fields.label: A choice about my body I made today
How it felt to notice that as my own choice
A boundary I held today
What supported me in holding it
What ownership over my body feels like right now

title: Compassion Toward the Body Practice
summary: A gentle acceptance-based practice for extending compassion toward a body that has been through harm.
goal: Support a client in extending compassion toward their body rather than treating it as separate or at fault.
body_md: Sexual abuse can leave a client relating to their own body with distance or blame, as though it were separate from them or somehow responsible, and this practice offers a slow, gentle way to extend compassion toward the body instead, a hand placed gently, a few kind words directed inward. Go at whatever pace feels tolerable and stop if it becomes too activating; this is stabilizing work, not exposure work.

fields.label: What it was like to bring compassion toward my body
Where I noticed resistance, if any
A kind word or phrase that felt true
How my body felt afterward
What I want to try again next time

title: Grounding Through Pacing Card
summary: A pocket card for pacing grounding skills so a client does not feel rushed through the process.
goal: Give a client control over the pace of their own grounding practice.
body_md: Being rushed through anything, including a coping skill, can itself feel unsafe for a client recovering from abuse, so this card is built around pacing: a menu of grounding options with permission to move as slowly as needed and to stop at any point. Complete this in session first, and let the client set the pace and choose which options to keep. 988 can be called or texted anytime support is needed between sessions.

fields.label: The grounding option I chose to start with
How the pace felt, too fast, too slow, or right
Where I chose to stop or pause
What helped me feel most in control of the pace
What I want on my own version of this card

title: Partner Patience and Pacing Agreement
summary: Has both partners agree on pacing around touch and closeness while one partner is healing.
goal: Give a couple a shared, explicit agreement about pacing physical closeness during healing.
body_md: A partner supporting someone healing from sexual abuse often wants to help but is unsure what is welcome, and guessing wrong can cause real hurt on both sides, so this sheet has both partners talk openly about pacing: what kinds of touch feel safe right now, what does not, and how to check in without it feeling like a test. Revisit the agreement as things shift, since pacing that works today may change.

fields.label: Partner healing: what feels safe to me right now
Partner healing: what does not feel safe right now
Supporting partner: how I will check in before touch
Supporting partner: what I need in order to keep checking in without frustration
How we will revisit this agreement as things change

title: Situation-Matched Coping Card Sort
summary: Sorts a client's existing coping skills by which type of situation each one actually fits best.
goal: Help a client match the right coping skill to the right kind of situation instead of using one skill for everything.
body_md: Clients often default to one familiar coping skill regardless of the situation, even when it is not the best fit, a calming skill used when what is actually needed is problem-solving, or vice versa. This sort has a client write out their coping skills on cards and sort them by situation type: needs calming, needs distraction, needs a decision. Use the sorted set to plan ahead for likely upcoming situations.

fields.label: A coping skill I use often
The type of situation it actually fits best
A situation where I used the wrong-fit skill by habit
A better-fitting skill for that situation
My sorted list by situation type

title: Coping Skill Barrier Troubleshoot Sheet
summary: Identifies what specifically gets in the way of using a known coping skill in the moment it is needed.
goal: Help a client troubleshoot why a known coping skill does not get used when it is actually needed.
body_md: A client often knows a coping skill well in theory but still does not reach for it in the moment it is needed, and this sheet digs into why: too complicated to remember, feels silly, not physically available, forgotten in the moment. Naming the specific barrier makes it possible to solve, whether that means simplifying the skill or building a reminder into the environment.

fields.label: The coping skill I know but do not use enough
What specifically gets in the way of using it
A way to make it simpler or more available
A reminder I could build into my day
What I want to try this week

title: Coping Skills as Acts of Care Practice
summary: Reframes coping skills as an expression of self-care values rather than a fix for a problem.
goal: Help a client experience coping skills as an act of care toward themselves rather than a chore.
body_md: Coping skills can start to feel like homework, one more task on a list, which paradoxically makes them harder to reach for, so this practice reframes each skill as an act of care a client is choosing to offer themselves, the same way they might offer it to someone they love. Pick one skill and practice it deliberately from that frame rather than from obligation, and notice whether it feels different.

fields.label: The coping skill I practiced from a place of care
What it felt like to frame it that way
How this compared with doing it out of obligation
A value this act of care connects to
What I want to bring this frame to next

title: Coping Recipe Steps Craft
summary: A child writes their own coping skill as a step-by-step recipe card to make it easy to follow.
goal: Give a child an easy-to-follow, personalized recipe for calming down.
body_md: Framing a coping skill as a recipe, with clear steps and a picture of the finished result, a calmer feeling, gives a young child something familiar and concrete to follow instead of an abstract instruction to calm down. The parent and child write the steps together and decorate the card like an actual recipe. Keep it somewhere the child can grab it when needed.

fields.label: Step one of my calm-down recipe
Step two of my calm-down recipe
What the finished result feels like
A time I used my recipe
What I want to change about the recipe

title: Coping Skill Charades Game
summary: Players act out a coping skill without speaking for the group to guess, followed by a real-life discussion.
goal: Use charades to make learning and remembering coping skills active and fun for a group.
body_md: A player draws a coping skill card and acts it out silently, deep breathing, counting, a favorite stretch, while the group guesses which skill it is, then the group briefly discusses when that skill might actually be useful for them. Acting the skill out physically tends to help it stick better than simply reading a list. Keep the pace playful and celebrate creative acting attempts.

fields.label: The skill I acted out
A skill I guessed correctly
A skill that was fun or funny to act out
When I might actually use one of the skills from the game
A skill I want to remember most

title: Feared Object Fact File Sheet
summary: Has a client research and record plain facts about a feared object or situation to sit alongside the fear.
goal: Give a client a factual counterweight to sit alongside an exaggerated feared image.
body_md: A phobia often runs on an exaggerated mental image of the feared object or situation, and this sheet has a client build a simple fact file, plain, verifiable information, to sit alongside that image rather than replace it outright. The point is not to argue the fear away but to give the client a second, factual reference point available when the exaggerated image takes over.

fields.label: The feared object or situation
A fact I found about it
Another fact I found
How the exaggerated image compares with the facts
What I want to remember when the fear spikes

title: Micro-Exposure Ladder Builder
summary: Builds an exposure ladder with steps small enough that the first one feels almost too easy.
goal: Help a client build a graded exposure ladder starting from a step that feels genuinely manageable.
body_md: A ladder with its first rung set too high often stalls before it starts, so this builder deliberately aims for a first step small enough to feel almost too easy, then works upward from there. A client lists the full range of situations connected to the fear, rates each for difficulty, and orders them into a ladder. Move up only once a rung feels manageable, not simply tolerable.

fields.label: The fear this ladder is built around
My first, easiest step
The next few steps in order of difficulty
The hardest step at the top
Which step I am ready to try next

title: Distress Tolerance for Exposure Card
summary: A pocket card of skills to use during an exposure step to stay with the discomfort rather than escape it.
goal: Give a client skills to stay present through an exposure step rather than leaving early.
body_md: Leaving an exposure step early because the discomfort feels unbearable can reinforce the fear rather than reduce it, so this card offers a short menu of distress tolerance skills, paced breathing, brief grounding, a coping statement, to help a client stay in the step a bit longer. The goal is staying with discomfort long enough for it to shift, not eliminating it.

fields.label: The exposure step I am working on
The skill I used to stay with it
Distress level at the start, 0 to 10
Distress level after staying with it
Whether I stayed as long as planned

title: Partner Cheerleader Not Rescuer Sheet
summary: Helps a supporting partner learn to encourage an exposure step rather than step in to rescue from it.
goal: Help a supporting partner learn to encourage rather than rescue during a phobia exposure step.
body_md: A supporting partner's instinct to protect can accidentally undercut an exposure step, stepping in to handle the feared thing before the client gets the chance to face it themselves. This sheet has both partners agree on what genuine encouragement looks like versus rescuing, and what signal the client can give if they truly do need the partner to step in. Practice the signal in advance.

fields.label: Partner facing the fear: what encouragement, not rescue, looks like to me
Partner facing the fear: my signal for if I truly need help
Supporting partner: what I will say instead of stepping in
Supporting partner: what makes it hard not to rescue
One agreement we are making about the next exposure step

title: Fear Ladder Board Game
summary: Players move a token up a drawn ladder board as they answer prompts about facing small fears.
goal: Use a simple board game to make talking about facing fears feel playful rather than heavy.
body_md: Players move a token up a drawn ladder by answering a prompt each turn, naming a fear, a step that would face it, or a time they were brave, with each correct or honest answer moving the token up one rung. Keep it light and let players choose how much detail to share. Whoever's token reaches the top first can cheer the rest of the group up the ladder too.

fields.label: A prompt I answered during the game
A fear I named
A step that would help face it
A time I was brave that I remembered during the game
How far my token climbed

title: Appearance Talk Awareness Sheet
summary: Logs how often a client talks about appearance, their own or others', to see how much airtime it takes up.
goal: Help a client see how much daily conversation and thought is going toward appearance.
body_md: Comments about appearance, one's own or someone else's, can become so routine they go unnoticed, quietly reinforcing how much attention the body's look receives relative to everything else. This sheet has a client log each appearance comment they make or hear across a week, then reflect on what that adds up to. The goal is awareness, not guilt about any single comment.

fields.label: An appearance comment I made or heard today
Whether it was about my own appearance or someone else's
How I felt saying or hearing it
A non-appearance comment I could offer instead next time
What I notice about the week's total

title: Function Over Appearance Practice
summary: Practices describing the body by what it does across a day rather than how it looks.
goal: Help a client build the habit of noticing their body by function rather than appearance.
body_md: Body image work often benefits from practicing an entirely different lens on the body, one built around function rather than appearance, and this practice has a client narrate their body's actions across an ordinary day, carrying groceries, laughing, climbing stairs, without any reference to how it looked doing so. Repetition matters more than any single entry; the lens takes practice to hold.

fields.label: Something my body did for me today
Another thing my body did for me today
How it felt to describe my body this way
A moment I noticed myself slipping back to appearance language
What I want to notice more of tomorrow

title: Nonjudgmental Body Scan Practice
summary: A brief mindfulness body scan practiced with nonjudgmental, descriptive language only.
goal: Give a client practice noticing the body with neutral, descriptive attention instead of evaluation.
body_md: A body scan practiced with strictly descriptive language, noticing warmth, tension or ease without labeling any of it good or bad, gives a client a different way of relating to their own body than the evaluative lens they usually bring. Guide the scan slowly through a few body areas, redirecting gently back to description any time a judgment slips in. This is a mindfulness skill, not a body-checking exercise.

fields.label: What I noticed in my body during the scan, described neutrally
A moment a judgment slipped in
How I redirected back to description
How this scan compared with how I usually relate to my body
What I want to practice noticing next time

title: My Body's Superpowers Drawing
summary: A child draws their body as having superpowers based on what it can do, not how it looks.
goal: Help a child build an early function-focused, playful relationship with their own body.
body_md: Framing the body's abilities as superpowers, running fast, hugging tight, climbing high, gives a young child a playful, function-focused way to think about their own body well before appearance-focused messages take hold more strongly. The parent and child draw the child as a superhero with powers based on real things the body can do. Keep the conversation led by what the child brings up.

fields.label: A superpower my body has
Another superpower my body has
How I drew myself using my superpowers
How my body helped me today
My favorite thing my body lets me do

title: Media Message Spot the Trick Game
summary: A group spots editing and marketing tricks in sample images to build media literacy around appearance.
goal: Use a group activity to build critical media literacy around appearance-focused images.
body_md: Players look at a set of sample images and try to spot the tricks used to shape how bodies appear, lighting, angles, editing, posing, earning a point for each trick correctly identified. The game builds a habit of critical viewing that can carry over to everyday media, gently loosening the pull of comparison. Debrief on how it felt to look at the images differently once the tricks were visible.

fields.label: A trick I spotted in one of the images
How the image looked different once I saw the trick
A trick I want to look for in media on my own now
How many points I earned
What I want to remember next time I compare myself to an image
